html:
The Nazca culture flourished on the dry south coast of Peru, in the river valleys of the Rio Grande de Nazca and Ica, from about 100 BCE to about 750 CE.

It grew out of the earlier Paracas culture, famous for its complex textiles (see Paracas textiles). The Nazca carried on that skill and added fine painted pottery in many colours, showing animals, plants, gods and trophy heads.

Two great works needed many hands:

  • The Nazca Lines: huge designs scraped into the desert floor, from straight lines kilometres long to a monkey, a spider and a hummingbird. They are best seen from the air. Their purpose is unknown; ideas include paths for ritual walks and links to water.
  • The puquios: underground channels that brought groundwater to fields in one of the driest places on Earth. Several dozen still work.

Nazca was probably not a single state but a group of chiefdoms sharing a culture and the ceremonial centre of Cahuachi. It overlapped in time with the Moche to the north. Around 500 to 750 CE the culture weakened, perhaps hit by floods and drought linked to El Niño, and the highland Wari empire took over the region.
sum: The Nazca culture flourished on the dry south coast of Peru, in the river valleys of the Rio Grande de Nazca and Ica, from about 100 BCE to about 750 CE.
